# Labour Party Manifesto 2005: Summary

## Core Vision and Values

The 2005 Labour manifesto, titled "Britain Forward, Not Back," centered on government's duty to provide opportunity and security for all in a changing world. The document outlined Labour's achievements since 1997 while setting ambitious goals for a potential third term, emphasizing the connection between economic dynamism and social justice.

## Economic Record and Plans

Labour highlighted unprecedented economic stability: the longest period of continuous growth in modern history, lowest sustained interest and inflation rates for a generation, and two million more people in employment since 1997. Their economic strategy focused on maintaining low debt and high employment, with a goal of raising the employment rate to 80 percent. They committed to not raising basic or top income tax rates and promised continued investment in public services through efficiency savings totaling £21 billion.

The manifesto emphasized supporting enterprise through improved skills training, science investment, and modernized transport infrastructure. They pledged £180 billion in transport investment through 2015 and promised to examine road pricing as a congestion solution.

## Education Reform

Education remained the stated top priority. Labour boasted that British ten-year-olds ranked third globally in literacy. Their plan focused on personalized learning, with goals including 85 percent of pupils achieving high standards at age eleven. They promised to make every secondary school an independent specialist school, expand the Academies program to 200 schools by 2010, and ensure no student dropped out at sixteen.

The manifesto committed to maintaining the maximum university fee at £3,000 (inflation-adjusted) and aimed for 50 percent of young people entering higher education by 2010.

## Healthcare

NHS spending had doubled since 1997 and would triple by 2008. Labour promised no one would wait more than 18 weeks from referral to treatment, with free choice of hospital. They planned to develop new community hospitals, expand NHS capacity through independent sector partnerships, and give patients greater choice over their care. Public health initiatives included restricting advertising of unhealthy foods to children and smoking bans in enclosed public places.

## Crime and Security

The manifesto highlighted a 30 percent reduction in crime since 1997 and promised a neighborhood policing team for every community. They pledged to increase Community Support Officers to 24,000 and introduce new powers to tackle antisocial behavior. Controversially, Labour committed to introducing ID cards backed by biometric data and a national register.

On immigration, they proposed a points-based system prioritizing skilled workers, with plans for fingerprinting visa applicants by 2008 and implementing electronic border tracking within five years.

## Family and Social Policy

Labour pledged to halve child poverty by 2010-11 and establish 3,500 Sure Start Children's Centers for under-fives. They promised to increase paid maternity leave to nine months by 2007, with a goal of one year by Parliament's end. Homeownership targets aimed for an additional one to two million homeowners.

## International Affairs

The manifesto defended Britain's EU membership and the Constitutional Treaty, promising a referendum. On defense, Labour supported maintaining the independent nuclear deterrent while modernizing armed forces. They committed to reaching the UN target of 0.7 percent of national income for development aid by 2013 and emphasized leadership on climate change and African development through the G8 presidency.

## Constitutional Reform

Labour promised to complete House of Lords reform, devolve more power to local authorities, and give neighborhoods greater control over local issues. They remained committed to the Human Rights Act while acknowledging the need to balance rights with responsibilities. A Commission on Equality and Human Rights would be established along with a Single Equality Act.
